apps.page_subtitle: api0 for AI agents, plus native desktop tools for Azure Integration Services and Git. All built in Rust.
apps.ais_runner_tagline: Azure Integration Services — local development desktop
apps.ais_runner_description: Run and test Azure Logic Apps locally without pushing to Azure. One-click Azurite + func start, live run history, workflow analysis bar, Service Bus queue counts, CI/CD DevOps view, Liquid template tester, and workflow chain graph — all in one desktop app.
apps.ais_monitor_tagline: Azure Logic Apps workflow chain explorer
apps.ais_monitor_description: Visualise how your Logic Apps connect to each other via Service Bus queues and Event Grid, inspect live run history per chain, trigger HTTP workflows with saved payloads, and monitor deployed workflow states — all from a single desktop view.
apps.ais_tracing_tagline: Correlation-id tracer for Azure Cosmos DB
apps.ais_tracing_description: Follow a single value — a correlation id, an order reference — through every container of an Azure Cosmos DB account, and see where it got to. Samples your containers, works out which field links documents together, then draws each step on a timeline. Empty rows matter as much as full ones: they show where the data hasn't arrived.
apps.ais_analytics_tagline: Correlation-id tracer for Azure Log Analytics
apps.ais_analytics_description: The same tracer, aimed at a Log Analytics workspace instead of Cosmos DB. Paste a correlation id and see every step it touched — it works out which column ties the steps of one flow together straight from the data, then draws where that value got to and where it didn't. An empty lane is as meaningful as a full one.
apps.blog_toolkit_tagline: AI-powered blog post manager with queue-to-publish workflow
apps.blog_toolkit_description: Write, generate, and schedule blog posts from your desktop. AI drafting via DeepSeek or Claude, markdown editor with live preview, queue-to-publish flow, weekly auto-publish, and multi-language support (FR/EN) — all in one native app.
apps.appscreens_tagline: The complete iOS & Android build and publish assistant
apps.appscreens_description: Your perfect companion for shipping mobile apps. Build, run, and iterate locally on iOS and Android, then package release artifacts ready for the App Store and Google Play. Handles bundle IDs, signing config, version bumps, screenshot generation in every required size, and the device-frame marketing assets — all from a single native desktop app.
apps.spreadwatch_tagline: Crypto price gaps across exchanges and Solana, live
apps.spreadwatch_description: Follow any crypto asset on Binance, Bybit, OKX, MEXC, Gate and Jupiter at once. See the best cross-venue edges net of fees, which venue's price trails the others, and the tokens Gate or MEXC just listed that Binance does not have yet. Swap SOL/USDT on-chain through Jupiter from a local hot wallet, in a dry run at every start and within hard limits.
apps.small_video_tagline: Record your screen, get a polished video: smooth cursor, zoom on clicks
apps.small_video_description: Record from the menu bar or with a shortcut. The cursor is redrawn so it glides, clicks become zooms that ease in, and a background, padding and rounded corners frame the result. Adjust it in the editor, cut the pauses, and export to MP4 at up to 4K.
apps.gitagent_tagline: Agentic graph for commit and deploy workflows
apps.gitagent_description: Turns a dirty working tree into an open pull request, one approved step at a time. Scans your repo, drafts a commit message and a PR description with a local ollama model or DeepSeek, then commits, pushes, and opens the PR — but nothing touches git history or the remote without an explicit yes at each gated step.
apps.splitter_tagline: Split long MP3/WAV recordings into tracks, from the keyboard
apps.splitter_description: Load a live set, a radio show or a digitised tape and get one file per track. Silence detection proposes the splits, you confirm or nudge each one by ear, then export: MP3 without re-encoding, or MP3/FLAC/WAV with loudness normalisation and ReplayGain tags. Can also pull the audio of a YouTube link.

solutions_azure.hero_title: Develop, monitor and trace Azure workflows locally
solutions_azure.hero_subtitle: Four native desktop apps for teams running Azure Integration Services. Test Logic Apps without pushing to the cloud, see how your workflows actually connect, and follow a single correlation id from one end of a chain to the other.
solutions_azure.friction_subtitle: Three things slow down most teams running Azure Integration Services.
solutions_azure.friction_1_body: Change a Logic App, push to Azure, wait, open the run history, read the error, repeat. A one-line fix costs minutes of cycle time — and you pay it every time.
solutions_azure.friction_1_outcome: Run the whole thing on your machine.
solutions_azure.friction_2_problem: Nobody can see the whole chain
solutions_azure.friction_2_body: Workflows hand off to each other through Service Bus queues and Event Grid topics. The portal shows you one workflow at a time and never the map, so the shape of the system lives in someone's head.
solutions_azure.friction_2_outcome: See the chain as a graph.
solutions_azure.friction_3_problem: A correlation id and nowhere to look
solutions_azure.friction_3_body: Something stopped halfway. The evidence is spread across Cosmos DB containers or Log Analytics tables, and the field that ties the steps together isn't the same one everywhere.
solutions_azure.friction_3_outcome: Follow the value on a timeline.
solutions_azure.tools_subtitle: Each tool covers one part of the loop. Use one on its own, or all four together.
solutions_azure.chooser_1_need: Run and test Logic Apps on my own machine
solutions_azure.chooser_2_need: See how workflows connect through Service Bus and Event Grid
solutions_azure.chooser_3_need: Trace a correlation id through Cosmos DB containers
solutions_azure.chooser_4_need: Trace a correlation id through a Log Analytics workspace
solutions_azure.stack_heading: Built in Rust, shipped as native desktop apps
solutions_azure.stack_body: Every tool is a single Rust binary with a Dioxus interface — no Electron, no runtime to install, no telemetry unless you opt in. They reach your subscription through the Azure CLI you have already authenticated, so no new credentials are stored. Every build is code-signed and notarized before it ships, so your OS verifies it on install.

solutions_azure.stack_point_2: Uses your existing Azure CLI session — no extra credentials
solutions_azure.stack_point_3: Code-signed and notarized builds, verified on install
solutions_azure.stack_point_4: Swiss-built, no telemetry unless you opt in

ais_runner.seo_title: AIS Runner — Run Azure Logic Apps Locally
ais_runner.seo_description: Desktop app for local Azure Logic Apps Standard development. One-click Azurite and Functions Core Tools, live run history, Liquid template testing and workflow chain graphs — without deploying to Azure.
overview: Developing Azure Logic Apps Standard normally means a slow loop: change a workflow, deploy it, trigger it, dig through the Azure portal to find out what happened, repeat. AIS Runner collapses that loop onto your own machine.

It starts the local stack for you — Azurite for storage emulation, Azure Functions Core Tools to host the workflow runtime — and then gives you the views the portal makes you hunt for: run history as it happens, how your workflows chain together, and what is sitting in your Service Bus queues.
It is a native desktop app written in Rust with Dioxus, so it starts instantly and stays out of the way of the rest of your toolchain.

features.title: Local stack from the toolbar
features.body: Azurite, the Service Bus Docker emulator, func start for Node.js workflows and mvn azure-functions:run for Java apps, each a button. func start runs pre-flight fixes first: package.json, connections.json ARM syntax, and stubs for missing settings.

features.title: Mock APIs
features.body: Scans every workflow.json, builds a contract of the outbound HTTP calls from adjacent Parse_JSON schemas, serves stubbed responses locally, and repoints the URL app settings at them. Stopping restores local.settings.json.

features.title: Record and replay tests
features.body: Capture a multi-step scenario — create a container, send a message, trigger a workflow — as plain JSON committed next to the workflows, then replay it with a live pass/fail per step, including waiting on a triggered run and asserting its outcome.

features.title: Live run history
features.body: Trigger any workflow with an auto-generated payload and watch the action timeline update in real time, with app logs filtered to just the workflow you selected.

features.title: Workflow analysis bar
features.body: Per workflow: trigger type, the Service Bus queues it reads and writes, blob containers, outbound HTTP calls and Liquid maps — so a workflow that silently never fires is visible rather than assumed working.

features.title: Connections and Liquid maps
features.body: Service Bus queues with message and dead-letter counts plus test sends, Cosmos DB, SQL, SFTP and blob browsing, and a maps tab that tests .liquid and .xslt templates against auto-suggested input on either DotLiquid or Liquid.

features.title: Azure DevOps view
features.body: Build pipelines grouped by folder, and a grid of build runs against release environments showing what is deployed where — queue a build from any branch, or click through to re-deploy a superseded run.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64

The installers handle the runtime dependencies: setup-linux.sh installs WebKitGTK, Node.js 20, Azure CLI, Azurite and Functions Core Tools on Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch; the Windows wizard offers the same in one step
Azure CLI signed in (az login) for the subscription-backed panels
A Logic Apps Standard project on disk, with a logic_apps/ folder
Docker, if you want the Service Bus emulator

faq.q: Does it need an Azure subscription?
faq.a: Not for local running — Azurite, the Service Bus emulator and Functions Core Tools cover that offline. The Connections and DevOps panels do read a real subscription through the Azure CLI, so those need az login.

faq.q: Does it change my workflow files?
faq.a: It reads and runs your Logic Apps Standard project. Two things it does write: starting Mock APIs rewrites the URL-shaped values in local.settings.json to point at the local mocks and restores the file on stop, and MSI connections are patched to local connection-string auth on every func start.

faq.q: How is this different from running func start myself?
faq.a: You can run func start yourself. What a terminal does not give you is the run history, the analysis bar, queue counts, the Liquid tester, the mock server and replayable scenarios in one place, refreshing as runs land.

faq.q: Can I verify what I downloaded?
faq.a: Yes. Each GitHub release carries a latest.json with the sha256 of every artifact.

ais_monitor.seo_title: AIS Monitor — Azure Logic Apps Workflow Chain Explorer
ais_monitor.seo_description: An operational console for Azure Logic Apps Standard workflow chains: chain graph, run history, config drift, RBAC and live diagnostics — as a desktop app and as a terminal companion for SSH sessions.
overview: A Logic Apps estate of any size stops being a list of workflows and becomes a graph: this workflow drops a message on a queue, that one picks it up, a third reacts to an Event Grid topic. The Azure portal shows you the workflows. It does not show you the graph.

AIS Monitor builds that graph from your deployed workflows and lets you walk it — pick a chain, see every run that flowed through it, drill into a run's action timeline, and trigger the entry point yourself with a payload you saved earlier.

It ships in two editions sharing one Azure backend and one on-disk cache: a desktop console with twelve tabs, and ais-monitor-tui, a single static binary for SSH sessions, jumpboxes and Windows Server where there is no desktop to run.

features.title: Workflow chain graph
features.body: Renders how deployed Logic Apps connect via Service Bus queues and Event Grid subscriptions, derived from the definitions by ais-chain rather than hand-drawn. Workflows linked by something undetectable, like a dynamic queue name, can be joined with a .ais-chain hint file.

features.title: Run history per chain
features.body: Follow one chain and see the runs of every workflow in it, in order, with per-run action timelines and KPIs — success rate, average and p95 duration, failure streak.

features.title: A terminal edition
features.body: ais-monitor-tui is a single static binary for machines with no desktop: chain browsing, run history and triggering over SSH, with a watch mode that auto-refreshes the focused step. Device-code sign-in covers hosts with no browser.

features.title: Config drift and health
features.body: Live app-settings values compared against App Configuration, managed-identity and app-setting health checks, and resource health across the whole group.

features.title: RBAC and cost
features.body: Managed identity role assignments in one view, plus a live log tail and month-to-date cost.

features.title: A dashboard that stays current
features.body: The home tab — failing workflows, live runs, dead letters, drift, RBAC gaps and cost together — polls in the background with adaptive backoff when Azure throttles, so it works unattended as a wall display.

features.title: Trigger panel
features.body: Fetch the callback URL for any HTTP-triggered workflow, edit the JSON payload in place, save named payloads per workflow, and watch the resulting run status appear live.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64 for the desktop console; the terminal edition runs anywhere its static binary does
Azure CLI signed in (az login) — both editions use your existing session
Reader on the resource group for read-only use: chains, KPIs, run and action detail, resources, observability, diagnostics
Contributor for the actions that change Azure state, plus User Access Administrator for the RBAC tab
A deployed Logic Apps Standard environment

faq.q: Can it change things in my Azure environment?
faq.a: Yes — this is not a read-only tool. The desktop console can trigger workflows, reset app settings, purge and requeue Service Bus messages, and assign RBAC roles. Each of those is gated behind a confirm dialog that shows the exact az command it is about to run, and read-only use needs only Reader.

faq.q: What is the difference between the desktop and terminal editions?
faq.a: The desktop console is the full twelve-tab tool. The terminal edition is deliberately smaller — chain browsing, run history and triggering for when there is no GUI available — not a shrunken copy of every tab. They share one Azure backend and one on-disk cache.

faq.q: Does it work against local workflows too?
faq.a: The desktop edition can scan a local logic_apps/ folder as well as a subscription, but it is aimed at deployed environments. For the local development loop, AIS Runner is the tool that covers that.

faq.q: How does it work out the chains?
faq.a: ais-chain reads the workflow definitions and matches the queues and topics one workflow writes to against the ones another triggers on. Nothing is configured by hand, though you can add a .ais-chain hint for links it cannot see.

faq.q: Why is run history slower than the rest?
faq.a: It goes through the Logic App's hostruntime API, which needs more than Reader and is throttled per subscription. The dashboard's background poll backs off automatically when it gets rate-limited.

ais_tracing.seo_title: AIS Tracing — Correlation ID Tracer for Azure Cosmos DB
ais_tracing.seo_description: Follow one correlation id or order reference through every container in an Azure Cosmos DB account and see exactly where it stopped. Automatic link-field detection, timeline view, missing steps shown as gaps.
overview: Something did not arrive. You have a correlation id, an order reference, or a customer number, and a Cosmos DB account with more containers than anyone remembers the shape of. The question is simple — how far did this value get? — and answering it usually means writing a query per container.

AIS Tracing answers it in one step. It samples your containers, works out on its own which field links documents to each other, then follows your value across all of them and draws each step on a timeline.
The gaps are the point. A step with no document is not an empty result to scroll past — it is the answer, showing you exactly which hop the data never reached.

features.title: Automatic link-field detection
features.body: Samples the containers and infers which field ties documents of one flow together, so you do not have to describe your schema to it first.

features.title: Account-wide search
features.body: One value, every container in the account, in a single pass — rather than a query per container written by hand.

features.title: Timeline view
features.body: Each step the value touched, in the order it happened, so latency between hops is visible rather than inferred from timestamps you compare manually.

features.title: Gaps as first-class results
features.body: Containers where the value never appeared are drawn as empty lanes. Where the trail stops is usually the whole answer.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64
Azure CLI signed in (az login) — the app has no login of its own and uses your existing session
An Azure Cosmos DB account you can read, including the separate Cosmos data-plane grant
Containers that carry some correlating field across documents

faq.q: Do I have to tell it my schema?
faq.a: No. It samples the containers and infers the linking field from the data, proposes a correlation key, and you paste a value to follow.

faq.q: A scan failed with 403 — what does that mean?
faq.a: Cosmos DB data access is a separate grant from normal Azure RBAC, so an account that can see the database still cannot read its contents. The app offers a button to give yourself the Built-in Data Reader role.

faq.q: Does it write to Cosmos DB?
faq.a: No. It is read-only against your account.

faq.q: What if my data is in Log Analytics rather than Cosmos DB?
faq.a: AIS Analytics is the same tracer pointed at a Log Analytics workspace.

faq.q: Will it work on a large account?
faq.a: It samples rather than scanning everything, so container count matters more than total document count. Very wide accounts take longer on the first pass.

ais_analytics.seo_title: AIS Analytics — Correlation ID Tracer for Azure Log Analytics
ais_analytics.seo_description: Paste a correlation id and see every step it touched across an Azure Log Analytics workspace. Works out the linking column from the data itself, then draws where the value got to and where it did not.
overview: The same problem as tracing through Cosmos DB, in the place most Azure integration telemetry actually lands: a Log Analytics workspace with more tables than anyone queries regularly.
Paste a correlation id. AIS Analytics works out from the data which column ties the steps of one flow together, then follows that value across the workspace and lays the result out as a timeline.
As with the Cosmos DB tracer, an empty lane carries as much information as a full one — it tells you which step never logged, which is usually the step that broke.

features.title: Column inference from data
features.body: Determines which column correlates the steps of a single flow by looking at the workspace, not at a configuration file you maintain.

features.title: Workspace-wide trace
features.body: One correlation id followed across the tables that matter, without composing a KQL query per table.

features.title: Timeline of steps
features.body: Every step the value touched, in order, so where time was spent is visible at a glance.

features.title: Two kinds of nothing, told apart
features.body: A lane with no rows is shown rather than omitted, and the view distinguishes a step the value has not reached yet from one that was never on its path — the difference between waiting and broken.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64
Azure CLI signed in (az login) — the app uses your existing session rather than its own login
An Azure Log Analytics workspace and read access to it

faq.q: Do I need to know KQL?
faq.a: No. Writing the queries is what the tool removes. Knowing KQL helps you interpret the tables, but you do not write anything to get a trace.

faq.q: How is this different from AIS Tracing?
faq.a: Same tracer, different backend. AIS Tracing reads an Azure Cosmos DB account; AIS Analytics reads a Log Analytics workspace. Teams that use both usually run both.

faq.q: Does it modify the workspace?
faq.a: No. It only runs read queries.

gitagent.seo_title: GitAgent — AI Commit Messages and Pull Requests, Gated by You
gitagent.seo_description: Turns a dirty working tree into an open pull request one approved step at a time. Drafts commit messages and PR descriptions with a local ollama model or DeepSeek — nothing touches git history or the remote without your explicit approval.
overview: Most AI git tooling has the same problem: it is either a text generator that hands you a commit message to paste, or an agent that runs commands on your repository and tells you afterwards. Neither is what you want on a repo you care about.

GitAgent models the work as a graph of steps — scan the tree, draft the commit message, commit, push, draft the PR description, open the PR — and stops at each one. You see what it proposes and what command it will run before it runs.
Drafting can run entirely on a local ollama model, which means the diff of a private repository never leaves your machine. DeepSeek is there if you would rather use a hosted model.

features.title: Approval at every step
features.body: Nothing touches git history or the remote without an explicit go-ahead on that specific step. The agent proposes; you approve.

features.title: Commit messages from the actual diff
features.body: Scans the working tree and drafts a message describing what changed, rather than restating the branch name.

features.title: PR descriptions
features.body: Drafts the pull request body from the commits on the branch, then opens the PR through the gh CLI.

features.title: Local model support
features.body: Point it at an ollama model running on your own machine and the contents of a private repository never leave it. DeepSeek is available as a hosted alternative.

features.title: The whole path in one place
features.body: Scan, commit, push and open the PR without switching between a terminal, a browser and a chat window.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64
git, and the GitHub CLI (gh) authenticated, for opening pull requests
Either ollama running locally, or a DeepSeek API key

faq.q: Can it push or rewrite history on its own?
faq.a: No. Every step that touches git history or the remote is gated behind an explicit approval for that step.

faq.q: Does my code get sent to a third party?
faq.a: Only if you choose a hosted model. With a local ollama model, drafting happens on your machine and the diff never leaves it.

faq.q: Does it work with GitLab or Bitbucket?
faq.a: Pull request creation goes through the GitHub CLI, so PR opening is GitHub-only today. The commit and push steps work on any git remote.

gitagent.pro_download_intro: Free for personal, educational and non-profit use, with 5 repositories. Commercial use — including a solo consultant on client work — requires GitAgent Pro, which also covers every repository, in every folder. Every build is produced by release CI and served from mayorana.ch.

Commercial use — including a solo consultant on client work and an employee using it at their job — requires GitAgent Pro, which also covers every repository. Pro is the commercial licence: there is nothing else to buy.

blog_toolkit.seo_title: Blog Toolkit — Desktop Blog Manager with AI Drafting
blog_toolkit.seo_description: Write, generate and schedule blog posts from a native desktop app. AI drafting via DeepSeek or Claude, markdown editor with live preview, queue-to-publish flow and weekly auto-publish in French and English.
overview: A blog that publishes on a schedule needs two things a text editor does not give you: somewhere for finished-but-unpublished posts to wait, and something that publishes them when the day comes.

Blog Toolkit is a native desktop app built around that queue. You draft in markdown with a live preview, optionally with an AI model doing the first pass, then move posts into a queue that publishes on its own schedule.
It handles both language versions of a post as part of the same flow, which is what makes a bilingual blog sustainable rather than something you keep meaning to catch up on.

features.title: Queue-to-publish flow
features.body: Finished posts wait in a queue instead of in a folder you forget about, and go out on the schedule you set.

features.title: Weekly auto-publish
features.body: Set the cadence once and the queue drains on its own. A week you do not write is a week the queue covers for you.

features.title: AI drafting
features.body: First drafts via DeepSeek or Claude, in the editor rather than in a separate chat window you copy out of.

features.title: Markdown editor with live preview
features.body: Write in markdown and see the rendered result as you type, including the code blocks that usually break in generic editors.

features.title: French and English side by side
features.body: Both locale versions of a post are managed together, so a translation does not drift a month behind the original.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64
A blog project laid out as content/{en,fr}/{queue,blog} — the app is asked for the project root on first launch
Node.js 18 or newer: publishing shells out to Node to rebuild the site index (the Windows installer and the macOS setup script handle this)
A DeepSeek or Anthropic API key, if you want AI drafting — pasted in Settings or read from DEEPSEEK_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

faq.q: Does it lock my content into a proprietary format?
faq.a: No. Posts are markdown files with frontmatter on your own disk. Publishing moves a file from the queue folder to the blog folder, sets its status and date, and rebuilds the index. The app manages the files; it does not own them.

faq.q: Can I use it without the AI features?
faq.a: Yes. The editor, queue and scheduler work with no model configured.

faq.q: Which models does it use?
faq.a: DeepSeek or Claude, chosen in Settings.

appscreens.seo_title: AppScreens — iOS and Android Build, Screenshot and Publish Assistant
appscreens.seo_description: Build and run iOS and Android apps locally, then package release artifacts for the App Store and Google Play. Handles bundle IDs, signing, version bumps, store screenshots in every required size and device-frame marketing assets.
overview: Shipping a mobile app release is a long list of small, exacting steps: bump the version, get the signing config right, produce a screenshot in each size the store demands, wrap them in device frames so the listing does not look amateur, then package the artifact the store will accept.
AppScreens does that list from one native desktop app, for both platforms, without the usual pile of shell scripts and half-remembered Xcode settings.
The screenshot generation alone is the part most teams do by hand every release, in every required size, for both stores.

features.title: Local build and run
features.body: Build, run and iterate on iOS and Android from one place, driving Xcode and Gradle underneath.

features.title: Release packaging
features.body: Produces the artifacts the App Store and Google Play accept, rather than leaving you to work out which archive format each one wants this year.

features.title: Bundle IDs, signing and version bumps
features.body: The configuration that breaks a release at the last minute, handled as part of the flow instead of remembered per release.

features.title: Store screenshots in every size
features.body: Generates the screenshot set both stores require, at every required resolution, from one capture.

features.title: Assets uploaded, not just generated
features.body: Device-framed screenshots go straight into App Store Connect and Google Play through their APIs, landing in the correct display type and screenshot set rather than waiting in a folder for someone to drag in.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon for iOS builds; Windows or Linux x86_64 for Android-only use
Xcode, for building and packaging iOS
The Android SDK and Gradle, for Android
An App Store Connect or Google Play account to publish the artifacts

faq.q: Can I use it for Android only?
faq.a: Yes. The Android path does not need macOS. iOS builds do, because Xcode does.

faq.q: Does it upload to the stores for me?
faq.a: Yes, for store assets: it talks to the App Store Connect and Google Play Developer APIs directly to upload screenshots into the right display types and sets. You supply the API credentials.

splitter.seo_title: Splitter — Split Long MP3 and WAV Recordings into Tracks
splitter.seo_description: Keyboard-driven desktop app to split live sets, DJ mixes and long recordings into tracks. Silence detection, split-by-split review, gapless MP3 export without re-encoding, FLAC/WAV, EBU R128 loudness and ReplayGain.
overview: A two-hour recording is one file, and what you want is twenty. Doing it in a waveform editor means scrolling, zooming, selecting and exporting by hand, twenty times, and hoping each cut landed in the gap and not on the first note.

Splitter reads the whole file once, suggests a split in every quiet stretch, then walks you through them: Tab plays three seconds either side of the next split, Enter keeps it, Backspace drops it. Most recordings are reviewed without touching the mouse.
Export copies the original MP3 frames instead of re-encoding them, with a gapless header, so the tracks sound exactly like the source and play back to back without a click.

features.title: Splits suggested, reviewed by ear
features.body: Silence detection proposes a split in the middle of every quiet stretch. You hear each one before you keep it, nudge it by 10 ms, or snap it to the quietest point nearby.

features.title: MP3 export without re-encoding
features.body: Original frames are copied and a LAME gapless header records the exact start and end, so tracks lose nothing and gapless players join them seamlessly. Tests compare every exported track with the source, sample by sample.

features.title: Other formats when you need them
features.body: MP3 VBR or CBR, FLAC or 16-bit WAV, with an A/B loop that switches between the original and the chosen format at the same position before you commit.

features.title: Loudness measured, not guessed
features.body: EBU R128 loudness and true peak for every track, updated as you move splits. ReplayGain 2.0 tags on export, and optional normalisation to −14 or −16 LUFS per track or for the whole set.

features.title: Silence trimmed at the edges
features.body: Lead-in, tail and the gaps between tracks are cut from the export by default, keeping a quarter of a second so quiet attacks and fades survive. Preview cuts plays exactly what the export will keep.

features.title: Titles, batches and YouTube links
features.body: Type titles as you go or paste a tracklist. Mark files done and export them all in one queue. Paste a YouTube link to download its audio and split it like any other file.

requirements: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows, or Linux x86_64
MP3 or WAV recordings; YouTube downloads arrive as audio and are opened directly
An internet connection only for the YouTube download, which fetches yt-dlp and Deno on first use

faq.q: Does it re-encode my MP3s?
faq.a: Not unless you pick another format. The default export copies the original MP3 frames, so the quality is exactly the source's.

faq.q: Is my original file changed?
faq.a: No. Splits and titles are saved in a small cutlist file next to your recordings, and tracks are written to a new folder. Apply cuts writes a separate copy.

faq.q: Will the tracks play without gaps?
faq.a: In gapless players — iTunes/Music, foobar2000, anything built on ffmpeg — yes: each track carries the header that tells the player where the audio really starts and ends.

faq.q: Do I need ffmpeg?
faq.a: No. Decoding, encoding and the YouTube download all work without installing anything else.

splitter.pro_download_intro: Free for personal, educational and non-profit use, exporting the first 10 tracks of each recording. Commercial use — including a solo consultant on client work — requires Splitter Pro, which also exports every track. Every build is produced by release CI and served from mayorana.ch.

Commercial use — including a solo consultant on client work and an employee using it at their job — requires Splitter Pro, which also exports every track. spreadwatch.seo_title: Spreadwatch — Crypto Spreads, Lead/Lag and New Listings Across Exchanges
spreadwatch.seo_description: Desktop app that quotes any crypto asset on Binance, Bybit, OKX, MEXC, Gate and Jupiter at once: cross-venue edges net of fees, which venue's price lags, and new Gate and MEXC listings Binance does not have yet.
overview: The same token trades on a dozen venues at slightly different prices, and the gap moves every second. Watching it means five exchange tabs, a DEX aggregator and a spreadsheet, and by the time the numbers are side by side they are stale.

Spreadwatch streams the order books of Binance, Bybit, OKX, MEXC and Gate, and polls Jupiter for Solana tokens, into one window. It shows the best buy-here, sell-there route in basis points, gross and net of the taker fee on both legs, and measures which venue's price tends to move last.

A second tab scans for tokens Gate or MEXC just listed against USDT that Binance spot does not list, and scores how serious each looks. For SOL/USDT, the app can also swap on-chain through Jupiter from a hot wallet it creates, signed on your machine.

features.title: One watchlist, six venues
features.body: Add any ticker (BTC, ETH, JUP, BONK…) and see its best bid and ask on Binance, Bybit, OKX, MEXC and Gate, plus Jupiter for Solana tokens, with a warning when a feed goes stale.

features.title: Edges net of fees
features.body: Every buy-on-one, sell-on-another route ranked in basis points, gross and after the taker fee on both legs, so a gap that fees would eat is shown for what it is.

features.title: Who is late
features.body: Measures, venue by venue, how many milliseconds its price trails the others on average — the venue that moves last is where a gap opens first.

features.title: New listings before Binance
features.body: Tokens Gate or MEXC listed in the last few days, or have scheduled, that Binance spot does not list, scored by volume, other listings, market cap and whether Binance already follows them through futures or Alpha.

features.title: On-chain swaps with guardrails
features.body: SOL/USDT swaps through Jupiter from a hot wallet the app creates. It starts in dry run every time, asks before going live, and enforces per-trade, daily, slippage and priority-fee limits a settings file can lower but never raise.

requirements: macOS 11 or later (Apple Silicon or Intel), Windows 10 or 11 with the WebView2 Runtime, or Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, current Fedora and Arch)
An internet connection: prices come from the exchanges' public APIs, no exchange account needed
For on-chain trading only: SOL in the app's hot wallet, and preferably a Solana RPC provider URL

faq.q: Do I need accounts or API keys on the exchanges?
faq.a: No. Prices come from the exchanges' public market data. Trading only happens on-chain through Jupiter, from the app's own wallet.

faq.q: Is a spread on screen a profit?
faq.a: No. The net figure subtracts taker fees, but not transfer times, withdrawal fees and limits, slippage or the price moving while you act. Spreadwatch shows where to look, not what you will earn. It is not financial advice.

faq.q: Where is my wallet key kept?
faq.a: In a file in the app's settings folder that only your user account can read, and nowhere else. Back it up: it is the only copy, and anyone who gets it can spend from the wallet.

spreadwatch.pro_download_intro: Free for personal, educational and non-profit use, following 3 assets at once. spreadwatch.pro_licence_body: Source-available under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0: free for personal use, learning, research and hobby projects, and for charities, schools, universities and government institutions, following 3 assets at once with every tab, every venue and trading. small_video.seo_title: Small Video — Screen Recorder with a Smooth Cursor and Auto-Zoom
small_video.seo_description: Desktop screen recorder for macOS and Windows: redrawn smooth cursor, automatic zoom on clicks, background and rounded corners, pauses cut out, MP4 export from 1080p to 4K.
overview: A raw screen recording is hard to watch: the cursor jumps around, the text is tiny, and every pause where you were thinking is still in it.

Small Video records the screen without the cursor and notes where the pointer goes. It then redraws a smooth cursor, zooms in where you clicked, and frames the video with a background, padding and rounded corners.
The editor lets you adjust each zoom, cut the silences and choose the frame. What you export is exactly what the preview shows.

features.title: Record from anywhere
features.body: Start and stop from the menu bar (macOS) or the notification area (Windows), or with ⌘⇧2 / Ctrl+Shift+2 from any app. The display your pointer is on is recorded with your microphone, and Small Video's own windows are left out.

features.title: A cursor that glides
features.body: The cursor isn't recorded: it's redrawn from the pointer's path, so it moves smoothly, and it can be made bigger.

features.title: Zooms from your clicks
features.body: Each click becomes a zoom that eases in on where you clicked. On the timeline you change when it starts and ends, how deep it goes and where it looks, or add one at the playhead with Z.

features.title: Pauses cut out
features.body: Silences where nothing is said are left out, picture and sound together, with a moment kept around your words. Two sliders set what counts as a pause, and a click on the timeline puts one back.

features.title: A frame for every format
features.body: Screen, 16:9, 9:16 or square, with background, padding, corners, shadow, cursor size and smoothing. Every change can be undone and is saved as you go.

features.title: Light files, sharp export
features.body: MP4 at 1080p, 1440p or 4K, 30 or 60 fps, with your voice. On macOS each recording is shrunk to about a fifth of its size right after you stop, with no visible loss on text.

requirements: macOS 15 or later on Apple Silicon, or Windows 10 (version 2004) or later
Screen Recording and Microphone permissions, asked for on the first recording
An internet connection on first export, to download the video tool (ffmpeg) the app uses

faq.q: Is the Windows version ready?
faq.a: It is built and signed with every release, but it hasn't been run on a real Windows machine yet, so expect rough edges. macOS is the tested platform.

faq.q: Does it work on Linux?
faq.a: Not yet. Under Wayland, an app can't read where the pointer is in other apps, and the redrawn cursor depends on it.

faq.q: Where are my recordings?
faq.a: Each recording is a folder in Movies/Small Video, with the video, the pointer movements and your edits. The exported MP4 is written next to it. Deleting a recording from the list moves it to the Trash, so you can still get it back.

faq.q: Do I need to install ffmpeg?
faq.a: No. The app downloads its own copy on first use and checks it against its published checksum. A copy already on your machine works too.

small_video.pro_download_intro: Free: export 10 different videos; exporting one again is free, and recording and editing are never limited. Pro: export every video, for personal or professional use. Every build is produced by release CI and served from mayorana.ch.
